items.stem: Importance of Classification : Grouping materials by properties helps study patterns and understand their uses. Mentions the ancient Indian Ayurveda system’s classification of matter based on 20 properties (guna). NCERT ACTIVITY Activity 6.1 : Let us identify Make a list of objects you see around and also write the names of the materials they are made up of in Table. Table : Identify materials I observe Materials they are made up of Based on everyday observations, one can conclude that objects are made up of various materials.
items.answer: To complete the activity:

items.stem: What did you learn from this activity?
items.answer: 1. According to the instructions, the objects were grouped based on a common property chosen from the list : shape, colour, hardness, softness, shine, dullness, or the materials they are made up of. (The specific one chosen would depend on the person doing the activity)..

items.stem: Why cannot a tumbler made of cloth be used for storing water?
items.answer: A tumbler needs to hold water without leaking and be reasonably rigid. Suitable materials include: Glass, Plastic, Metal (like stainless steel or aluminum) Ceramic / Pottery (Possibly very thick, waterproofed paper/ cardboard)

items.stem: Identify the ball that achieves the highest bounce. Figure : Different types of balls used for various purposes Table : Bouncing level of the balls Ball Bounce (high, medium or low) Tennis ball Cricket ball
items.answer: Ball Bounce (high, medium or low) Tennis ball High Cricket ball Low The Tennis ball achieves the highest bounce. Reason : This is because the Tennis ball is made primarily of rubber, which is a highly elastic material designed to bounce well. The Cricket ball is made of harder, less elastic materials (cork, string, leather) and is designed for durability rather than high bounce. Activity 6.5 : Let us observe

items.stem: Compare your observations with the observations of your friends and discuss. Table : Hard or soft objects and the materials they are made up of Object Hard/Soft Material(s) Brick Hard Baked clay Water bottle Pillow Tumbler Table Sweater Any other
items.answer: Object Hard/Soft Material(s) Brick Hard Baked clay Water bottle Hard Plastic, Metal (like steel/aluminum), Glass Pillow Soft Cloth (outer); Cotton, Foam, Feathers (inner) Tumbler Hard Glass, Plastic, Metal (like steel), Ceramic Table Hard Wood, Metal, Plastic, Glass (sometimes tabletop) Sweater Soft Wool, Cotton, Acrylic, other synthetic fibres Any other (Depends) (Depends on the object chosen) Activity 6.6 : Let us classify Classify the following objects as transparent, translucent or opaque in Table. Table : Classification of objects Transparent Translucent Opaque

items.stem: Write down your observations in Table. Table : Mixing different materials in water Material Prediction (Will disappear/will not disappear in water) Observation (Disappears in water/ does not disappear in water) Sugar Salt Chalk powder Sand Sawdust Any other
items.answer: Material Prediction (Will disappear/will not disappear in water) Observation (Disappears in water/ does not disappear in water) Sugar Will disappear Disappears in water (Soluble) Salt Will disappear Disappears in water (Soluble) Chalk powder Will not disappear Does not disappear in water (Insoluble - forms suspension) Sand Will not disappear Does not disappear in water (Insoluble - settles down) Sawdust Will not disappear Does not disappear in water (Insoluble - floats) Any other (Depends) (Depends on the substance) Activity 6.8 : Let us measure

items.stem: Compare the data and infer which is heavier or lighter.
items.answer: This activity compares the mass (weight) of equal volumes of different materials. Prediction : You need to predict the order from lightest to heaviest based on experience. Most people would predict: Lightest : Cup A (Water) Heavier : Cup B (Sand) Heaviest : Cup C (Pebbles) Observation/Inference (after weighing) : When weighed on a balance, you would typically find that for the same volume (half a cup): Cup C (Pebbles) has the most mass (is the heaviest). Cup B (Sand) has intermediate mass. Cup A (Water) has the least mass (is the lightest). Therefore, the inference confirms the prediction : Pebbles > Sand > Water in terms of heaviness for the same volume.

items.stem: Visit your kitchen and observe how your parents have organized various edibles. Can you suggest a better sorting method?
items.answer: Sort items by state and use: Group Examples Container / Shelf & Reason Dry grains & pulses rice, wheat, lentils Airtight jars – keep moisture and insects out Spices & masalas turmeric, chilli, cumin Small transparent bottles on a spice-rack – quick to identify Snacks biscuits, chips, nuts Clip-lid boxes – stay crisp Breakfast & instant foods oats, noodles, cereals Same shelf – saves morning time Liquids oil, vinegar, sauces Taller shelf – avoids leakage onto dry foods Festive/ occasional items sweets moulds, dry fruits Top shelf – frees daily-use space

items.stem: The containers used to store materials in shops and homes are usually transparent. Give reasons.
items.answer: Easy identification, quick stock check, early spoilage detection, and customer trust—all possible because light passes through transparent material.

items.stem: State whether the statements given below are True [T] or False [F]. Correct the False statement(s). (i) Wood is translucent while glass is opaque. [ ] (ii) Aluminium foil has lustre while an eraser does not. [ ] (iii) Sugar dissolves in water whereas sawdust does not. [ ] (iv) An apple is a matter because it occupies no space and has mass. [ ].
items.answer: (i) False – wood is opaque; glass is transparent. (ii) True. (iii) True. (iv) False – an apple occupies space and has mass.

items.stem: We see chairs made up of various materials, such as wood,iron, plastic, bamboo, cement and stones. Following awesome desirable properties of materials which can be used to make chairs. Which materials used to make chairs fulfil these properties the most? (i) Hardness (does not bend or shake on sitting even after long use). (ii) Lightweight (easy to lift or to take from one place to another). (iii) Does not feel very cold when sitting during winters. (iv) Can be cleaned regularly and made to look new even after long use.
items.answer: (i) Hardness : Iron (also cement/stone) (ii) Light-weight : Bamboo or plastic (iii) Not cold in winter : Wood, bamboo or plastic (iv) Easy to clean & look new : Plastic or powder- coated/painted iron

items.stem: You need to have containers for collection of : (i) Food waste, (ii) Broken glass and (iii) Wastepaper. Which materials will you choose for containers of these types of waste? What properties of materials do you need to think of?
items.answer: Choosing good waste containers

items.stem: Air is all around us but does not hinder us from seeing each other. Whereas, if a wooden door comes in between, we cannot see each other. It is because air is __________ and the wooden door is __________. Choose the most appropriate option: (i) Transparent, opaque (ii) Translucent, transparent (iii) Opaque, translucent (iv) Transparent, translucent
items.answer: (i) Transparent, opaque. Air is transparent (light passes straight through it) and the wooden door is opaque (it blocks light).

items.stem: Imagine you have two mysterious materials, X and Y. When you try to press material X, it feels rigid and does not change its shape easily. On the other hand, material Y easily changes its shape when you press it. Now, when you mix both materials in water, only material X dissolves completely, while material Y remains unchanged. What can materials X and Y be? Can you identify whether material X is hard or soft? What about material Y? Justify your answer.
items.answer: 1. Material X could be common salt. It is hard (keeps its shape when pressed) and soluble (dissolves fully in water).

items.stem: Who am I? Identify me on the basis of the given properties. me. (ii) Make your own ‘Who am I?’

options.label: C
options.text: I am hard and soluble in water

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot see clearly through me. (e) I have mass and volume but you cannot see

items.answer: (a) Shiny (lustrous) " Aluminium foil (b) Easy to squeeze " Sponge (c) Hard and dissolves in water " Table salt (d) Cannot see clearly through it " Butter paper / frosted glass (e) Has mass and volume but cannot be seen " Air

items.stem: You are provided with the following materials— vinegar,honey, mustard oil, water, glucose and wheat flour. Make any two pairs of materials where one material is soluble in the other. Now, make two pairs of materials where one material remains insoluble in the other material.
items.answer: Soluble pairs :

items.stem: What is a material as defined in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Any object that has a specific shape and color

options.label: B
options.text: Any substance that is used to create an object

options.label: C
options.text: Only substances that are hard and shiny

options.label: D
options.text: Only substances that are naturally occurring

items.answer: (B) Any substance that is used to create an object. A material is any substance used to make or construct an object, with common examples including paper, wood, glass, and plastic..

items.stem: According to Rasaratnasamuchchaya, as mentioned in the chapter, what materials are used to make a crucible?
items.answer: (C) Clay and iron A shloka from the Rasaratnasamuchchaya mentions that clay and iron are the materials used to make a crucible, a vessel designed for melting substances.

items.stem: What can be concluded from the everyday observation that objects around us are made of paper, wood, cloth, glass, etc.?

options.label: A
options.text: All objects are made from a single type of material

options.label: B
options.text: Objects are made up of various materials

options.label: C
options.text: Only natural materials are used to make objects

options.label: D
options.text: Materials cannot be seen, only the objects they form

items.answer: (B) Objects are made up of various materials. Our daily experiences show that different objects are constructed using a diverse range of materials, each chosen for its specific properties suited to the object’s purpose.

items.stem: What is classification in the context of objects or materials?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of using objects for different purposes

options.label: B
options.text: The method of arranging objects or materials into groups based on common properties

options.label: C
options.text: The study of the chemical composition of materials

options.label: D
options.text: The way objects change their shape over time

items.answer: (B) The method of arranging objects or materials into groups based on common properties. Classification is the systematic arrangement of objects or materials into groups or categories based on shared characteristics, similarities, or differences, which helps in organizing and studying them.

items.stem: During which ancient civilization did pottery techniques become further sophisticated, with bright red surfaces painted with black-coloured designs?
items.answer: (C) Sindhu-Sarasvati (Harappan) Civilisation Pottery techniques became highly advanced during the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation (2600– 1900 BCE), featuring decorative painting with geometric patterns and animal designs on bright red surfaces..

items.stem: What determines the choice of material for making a specific object?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the color and cost of the material

options.label: B
options.text: The availability of the material in a specific region

options.label: C
options.text: The material’s properties and the intended purpose of the object

options.label: D
options.text: The ease with which the material can be broken

items.answer: (C) The material’s properties and the intended purpose of the object. Materials are chosen based on whether their inherent properties (like strength, flexibility, transparency) are suitable for the function the final object is meant to perform.

items.stem: Why can a tumbler made of cloth NOT be used for storing water?

options.label: A
options.text: Cloth is too heavy to make a tumbler

options.label: B
options.text: Cloth is not capable of holding water as it is porous

options.label: C
options.text: Cloth tumblers are not aesthetically pleasing

items.answer: (B) Cloth is not capable of holding water as it is porous. A tumbler for storing water needs to be made from a material that is waterproof and can contain liquids. Cloth is porous and would allow water to seep through.

items.stem: What is a key difference in appearance between freshly cut wood and iron?

options.label: A
options.text: Freshly cut wood is shiny, while iron is dull

options.label: B
options.text: Freshly cut wood has a distinct appearance quite different from that of iron

options.label: C
options.text: Both freshly cut wood and iron always look identical

options.label: D
options.text: Iron is always soft, while freshly cut wood is always hard

items.answer: (B) Freshly cut wood has a distinct appearance quite different from that of iron. Materials often have different visual characteristics. Freshly cut, unpolished wood has a look that is clearly distinguishable from the appearance of a metal like iron.

items.stem: What term is used to describe materials that typically have shiny surfaces?
items.answer: (C) Lustrous Materials that possess a natural shine or gleam on their surface are said to have a lustrous appearance. Many metals exhibit this property.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a non- lustrous material?
items.answer: (C) Paper Non-lustrous materials are those that do not have a shiny surface. Paper, along with wood and rubber, is cited as an example of a non-lustrous material.

items.stem: Why might some metals lose their lustre and appear dull over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they absorb too much light

options.label: B
options.text: Due to the effect of air and moisture on their surface

options.label: C
options.text: Because they are polished too frequently

items.answer: (B) Due to the effect of air and moisture on their surface. Some metals react with components of the air (like oxygen) and moisture, forming a layer on their surface (e.g., tarnish or rust) that makes them appear dull and lose their original shine.

items.stem: How are soft materials characterized?

options.label: A
options.text: Materials that are always shiny and smooth

options.label: B
options.text: Materials which can be compressed or scratched easily

options.label: C
options.text: Materials that are difficult to bend or break

options.label: D
options.text: Materials that are good conductors of heat

items.answer: (B) Materials which can be compressed or scratched easily. Soft materials are those that respond easily to pressure they can be compressed or scratched with little effort.

items.stem: What is the main difference between transparent and opaque materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Transparent materials are always hard; opaque materials are always soft

options.label: B
options.text: Things can be seen clearly through transparent materials; not at all through opaque materials

options.label: C
options.text: Transparent materials reflect all light; opaque materials absorb all light

options.label: D
options.text: Transparent materials are man-made; opaque materials are natural

items.answer: (B) Things can be seen clearly through transparent materials; not at all through opaque materials. Transparent materials, like clear glass or air, allow light to pass through them without significant scattering, so objects can be seen clearly. Opaque materials, like wood or metal, block light, preventing visibility through them.

items.stem: What are translucent materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Materials through which objects can be seen clearly

options.label: B
options.text: Materials through which objects cannot be seen at all

options.label: C
options.text: Materials through which objects can be seen, but not clearly

options.label: D
options.text: Materials that produce their own light

items.answer: (C) Materials through which objects can be seen, but not clearly. Translucent materials allow some light to pass through, but they scatter it, so objects viewed through them appear blurry or indistinct. Butter paper is an example.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of an opaque material?
items.answer: (D) Wood Wood is an opaque material because light cannot pass through it, and therefore, one cannot see through a wooden object like a closed door.

items.stem: Ghulan hides behind a wall, Sheeta hides behind a big tree, and Sara hides behind a frosted glass door during a game of hide and seek. Sheeta’s younger brother is watching them through a clear glass window. Which child is hiding behind a translucent material?
items.answer: (C) Sara Sara hides behind a frosted glass door. Frosted glass is an example of a translucent material, through which objects can be seen, but not clearly. The wall and tree are opaque, and the clear window is transparent.

items.stem: What happens to materials that are soluble in water when mixed with it?

options.label: A
options.text: They float on the surface of the water

options.label: B
options.text: They settle down at the bottom of the container

options.label: C
options.text: They completely disappear or dissolve in the water

options.label: D
options.text: They change the color of the water to black

items.answer: (C) They completely disappear or dissolve in the water. Soluble materials are those that mix uniformly with water to form a solution, causing them to seem to disappear as their particles disperse throughout the water.

items.stem: What are materials that do not mix with water and do not disappear even after stirring for a long time called?
items.answer: (C) Insoluble in water Materials that do not dissolve in water, even after prolonged stirring, and remain as separate particles or layers are termed insoluble in water. Sand is an example.

items.stem: What are two common household substances that dissolve in water to make shikanji (lemonade)?
items.answer: (B) Sugar and salt In the example of making shikanji, Ghulan’s mother mixes sugar and salt in water and Ghulan notices that these substances disappear after a while, meaning they dissolve.

items.stem: If you mix sand with water and stir it, what will you observe after some time?

options.label: A
options.text: The sand will completely dissolve and disappear

options.label: B
options.text: The sand will float on the surface of the water

options.label: C
options.text: The sand will settle down at the bottom as it is insoluble

options.label: D
options.text: The water will turn into a sandy gel

items.answer: (C) The sand will settle down at the bottom as it is insoluble. Sand is insoluble in water. When mixed and stirred, the sand particles will temporarily suspend but will eventually settle at the bottom of the container once left undisturbed.

items.stem: The one which is heavier has more mass and the one which is lighter has less mass. What property is being referred to here?
items.answer: (C) Mass Mass is the measure of the amount of matter in an object. An object that feels heavier (when comparing equal volumes or in general) typically has more mass than one that feels lighter.

items.stem: What is volume of an object or substance?

options.label: B
options.text: The amount of matter it contains

options.label: C
options.text: The space occupied by the object or substance

options.label: D
options.text: Its ability to dissolve in water

items.answer: (C) The space occupied by the object or substance. Volume is the measure of the three-dimensional space that an object or substance takes up. It indicates how much room it occupies.

items.stem: What are the standard SI units used to measure mass, as mentioned in the context of matter?
items.answer: (C) Gram (g) and kilogram (kg) Mass indicates the amount of matter in an object, and it is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg), with the kilogram being the SI unit.

items.stem: What are the two fundamental properties that all matter possesses?
items.answer: (C) Mass and volume (occupies space) Matter is defined as anything that has mass and takes up space these two characteristics, mass and volume, are what define it.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : A tumbler made of glass can hold water. Reason (R) : Glass is a transparent and hard material.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (B) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A glass tumbler can hold water because glass is non-porous and waterproof. While glass is also transparent and hard, these properties are not the primary reasons it can hold water, though hardness contributes to its structural integrity.

items.stem: Transparency (ability to see through clearly) Which of these properties can be used to classify or group materials?
items.answer: (D) 1, 2, and 3 Materials can be grouped based on properties such as appearance (lustre), texture (hardness or softness), and visibility through them (transparency, translucency, or opacity). All three are valid criteria for classification.

items.stem: A student is given three balls of the same size: one made of rubber (tennis ball), one of leather (cricket ball), and one of soft plastic (hand exercise ball). When dropped from the same height, the tennis ball bounces the highest. This activity primarily helps in understanding that:

options.label: B
options.text: Different materials have different properties (e.g., elasticity affecting bounce)

options.label: C
options.text: The color of the ball determines its bounce

items.answer: (B) Different materials have different properties (e.g., elasticity affecting bounce). The varying bounce heights of balls made from different materials, despite being the same size, demonstrate that the choice of material imparts specific properties (like elasticity) to the object, affecting its performance.

items.stem: What is terra-cotta, as mentioned in the context of ancient pottery?

options.label: C
options.text: A special kiln for baking pottery

items.answer: (B) Baked clay. Clay used for pottery was eventually hardened by baking it in kilns, and the resulting material is known as ‘terra-cotta’.

items.stem: Why is it not a good idea to use paper-like materials for making cooking utensils?

options.label: B
options.text: Paper is not good at holding food items

options.label: C
options.text: Paper cannot withstand high cooking temperatures and is not waterproof

options.label: D
options.text: Paper utensils are difficult to clean

items.answer: (C) Paper cannot withstand high cooking temperatures and is not waterproof. Cooking utensils must be able to endure high heat without burning or deforming and must be able to hold liquids and food. Paper lacks these essential properties.

items.stem: Materials which can be compressed or scratched easily are called:
items.answer: (C) Soft materials Soft materials are described as those that can be easily squeezed or have surfaces that are easily scratched.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of a transparent material?
items.answer: (C) Air Air allows light to pass through it clearly, enabling us to see objects without obstruction, making it a transparent material.

items.stem: What is the main difference between a lustrous material and a non-lustrous material?

options.label: A
options.text: Lustrous materials are always metals; non- lustrous are never metals

options.label: B
options.text: Lustrous materials have a shiny surface; non- lustrous materials have a dull surface

options.label: C
options.text: Lustrous materials are always hard; non- lustrous materials are always soft

options.label: D
options.text: Lustrous materials are soluble in water; non- lustrous materials are insoluble

items.answer: (B) Lustrous materials have a shiny surface; non- lustrous materials have a dull surface. Lustre refers to the shininess of a material’s surface. Lustrous materials reflect light well and appear shiny, while non-lustrous materials have a dull appearance and do not reflect light as effectively.

items.stem: All of the following are properties used to classify materials EXCEPT:
items.answer: (D) Electrical conductivity Materials are classified based on properties such as appearance, hardness, transparency, solubility, and mass or volume. While electrical conductivity is a property of materials, it is not a main criterion emphasized in this particular discussion.

items.stem: If a shopkeeper stores spices in one corner of the shop and pulses in another, what principle of organizing materials is being applied?

options.label: B
options.text: Classification based on common properties or type

items.answer: (B) Classification based on common properties or type Grouping similar items together, like spices with spices and pulses with pulses, is an application of classification. This makes it easier to locate and manage items.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Some metals develop a dull appearance over time. Reason (R) : This is due to the effect of air and moisture reacting with the metal surface.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Many metals lose their initial lustre because their surfaces react with oxygen and moisture in the atmosphere, forming a layer of oxide or tarnish which appears dull.

items.stem: Only the cheapest available material is selected.
items.answer: (A) 1 and 2 only The selection of a material for an object depends critically on its inherent properties (e.g., strength, flexibility) and how well these properties suit the object’s intended use. Cost can be a factor, but it’s not the sole or primary determinant if the material isn’t functional.

items.stem: A student is making a list of materials that can be used to make a window pane through which one can see clearly outside. Which property is most crucial for the window pane?
items.answer: (C) Transparency For a window pane intended for clear viewing, the most important optical property is transparency, which allows light to pass through without significant scattering, enabling a clear view of objects on the other side.

items.stem: What material property is primarily being tested when you try to scratch the surface of an object with a metal key?
items.answer: (C) Hardness Scratching a material is a common way to assess its relative hardness. Materials that are difficult to scratch are considered hard, while those that scratch easily are softer.

items.stem: Why does oxygen gas dissolving in water play an important role for aquatic life?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the water shiny and attractive

options.label: B
options.text: It is essential for the survival (respiration) of animals and plants living in water

options.label: C
options.text: It helps to keep the water warm

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents the water from becoming salty

items.answer: (B) It is essential for the survival (respiration) of animals and plants living in water. Aquatic organisms, like fish and many underwater plants, require dissolved oxygen for respiration, which is the process of releasing energy from food. The solubility of oxygen in water is thus vital for their survival.

items.stem: In the context of Arrived, what does the term guna refer to ?
items.answer: (B) Properties of matter Arrived uses a framework of 20 properties (guna), arranged in ten opposing pairs, to describe all forms of physical matter, including living organisms and food.

items.stem: What is the SI unit for volume, as stated in the Do you know? box?
items.answer: (C) Cubic metre m3 The Do you know? box specifies that the SI unit for volume is the cubic metre, abbreviated as m3 . While litre and milliliter are common units for volume, cubic metre is the SI standard.

items.stem: How does a soluble material like sugar behave in water compared to an insoluble material like sand?

options.label: B
options.text: Sugar dissolves and disappears, while sand does not dissolve and settles

options.label: C
options.text: Sugar changes water color, while sand makes water cloudy

options.label: D
options.text: Sugar makes water hard, while sand makes water soft

items.answer: (B) Sugar dissolves and disappears, while sand does not dissolve and settles. Sugar is soluble and its particles disperse uniformly in water, making it seem to disappear. Sand is insoluble and its particles will remain distinct, eventually settling at the bottom.

items.stem: Which of these materials would NOT be suitable for making a container to hold liquids?

options.label: D
options.text: Unglazed clay pot (if pores are not sealed)

items.answer: (D) Unglazed clay pot (if pores are not sealed) Glass, metal, and most plastics are impervious to liquids. An unglazed clay pot, however, can be porous and allow water to seep through, unless it has been treated or glazed to be waterproof.

items.stem: If an object is described as mridu (soft) and laghu (light in weight) according to Archived properties, what might be an example of such an object?
items.answer: (B) A cotton ball A cotton ball is soft (can be easily compressed) and light in weight, fitting the Archived descriptions of mridu and laghu. The other options are generally harder or heavier.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Air is considered matter. Reason (R) : Air occupies space and has mass.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Matter is defined as anything that occupies space (has volume) and has mass. Air fulfills both these criteria; for example, an inflated balloon shows air occupies space and has mass.

items.stem: All materials have exactly the same properties.
items.answer: (A) 1 and 2 only It’s common for an object (like a chair) to be made from various materials (wood, plastic, metal). Similarly, a single material (like plastic) can be used to make many different objects (bottles, toys, pens). Materials differ widely in their properties.

items.stem: A chef needs a material for a frying pan that can withstand high heat and conduct heat efficiently to cook food. Which material property is most critical for this application?

options.label: C
options.text: Ability to withstand high temperatures and conduct heat

items.answer: (C) Ability to withstand high temperatures and conduct heat A frying pan must not melt or deform at cooking temperatures and needs to conduct heat effectively from the stove to the food. Copper is a good choice for this, while wood and plastic are not suitable.

items.stem: In ancient Indian pottery, what were slips used for?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the clay softer for kneading

options.label: B
options.text: As a fuel for the kilns

options.label: C
options.text: As protective or decorative coats of multiple colours applied to pottery

options.label: D
options.text: To help turn the pottery wheel smoothly

items.answer: (C) As protective or decorative coats of multiple colours applied to pottery. About 4000 BCE onwards, Sindhu-Sarasvati potters developed techniques including the application of ‘slips’, which were protective or decorative coats in various colours.

items.stem: When classifying objects, why is it useful to group them based on the materials they are made of?

options.label: A
options.text: It helps determine the age of the objects

options.label: B
options.text: Objects made of the same material often share similar properties and uses

options.label: C
options.text: It is the only way to count the total number of objects

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the objects look more organized aesthetically

items.answer: (B) Objects made of the same material often share similar properties and uses. Grouping by material helps in understanding patterns. Objects made from the same material (e.g., all metal objects) will likely share common characteristics (like hardness, lustre, conductivity) and potential uses.

items.stem: The property of a material that describes whether it is rough or smooth to touch is called its:
items.answer: (B) Texture Texture refers to the surface quality of a material that can be perceived by touch, such as being rough, smooth, coarse or fine.

items.stem: What is any substance used to create an object referred to as?
items.answer: Any substance used to create an object is referred to as material.

items.stem: Name one material that the earliest pottery found in the Indian subcontinent was made from.
items.answer: Clay.

items.stem: What is baked clay called?
items.answer: Baked clay is called terra-cotta.

items.stem: What is the method of arranging objects into groups based on common properties called?
items.answer: The method of arranging objects into groups is called classification.

items.stem: What property should a material have to make a tumbler for holding water?
items.answer: The material should be capable of holding water.

items.stem: Can an object be made from different materials?
items.answer: Yes, an object can be made from different materials.

items.stem: What are materials with shiny surfaces said to have?
items.answer: Materials with shiny surfaces are said to have a lustrous appearance.

items.stem: Give one example of a metal.
items.answer: Iron (or copper, zinc, aluminium, gold).

items.stem: What are materials that do not have a shiny surface called?
items.answer: Materials that do not have a shiny surface are called non-lustrous materials.

items.stem: What are materials that can be compressed or scratched easily called?
items.answer: Materials which can be compressed or scratched easily are called soft materials.

items.stem: What are materials through which things can be seen clearly called?
items.answer: Materials through which things can be seen clearly are called transparent materials.

items.stem: Give one example of an opaque material.
items.answer: Wood (or cardboard, metals).

items.stem: What are materials through which objects can be seen, but not clearly, known as?
items.answer: Materials through which objects can be seen, but not clearly, are known as translucent materials.

items.stem: What happens to sugar when it is mixed in water and stirred?
items.answer: Sugar disappears or dissolves in water.

items.stem: What are materials that do not mix with water called?
items.answer: Materials that do not mix with water are called insoluble in water.

items.stem: Which gas, dissolved in water, is very important for the survival of aquatic animals and plants?
items.answer: Oxygen gas.

items.stem: What property of an object is described by how heavy or light it is?
items.answer: Mass.

items.stem: What does the space occupied by water in a tumbler represent?
items.answer: The space occupied by water represents its volume.

items.stem: What are the two fundamental properties possessed by all materials, leading to the definition of matter?
items.answer: Mass and volume.

items.stem: What is anything that occupies space and has mass called?
items.answer: Anything that occupies space and has mass is called matter.

items.stem: What determines the choice of material for making an object?
items.answer: The choice of material depends on its properties and the purpose for which the object is to be used.

items.stem: Why can a tumbler not be made of cloth for storing water?
items.answer: A cloth tumbler cannot be used for storing water because cloth is not capable of holding water; water would seep through it.

items.stem: What is lustre in materials? Name two metals that have lustre.
items.answer: Lustre is the shiny appearance of a material. Iron and copper are examples of metals that usually have lustre.

items.stem: Why do some metals lose their lustre over time?
items.answer: Some metals lose their lustre and look dull due to the effect of air and moisture on their surfaces over time.

items.stem: Differentiate between hard and soft materials using the property of compressibility.
items.answer: Soft materials can be easily compressed or scratched, like an eraser. Hard materials are difficult to compress or scratch, like a stone.

items.stem: Give an example that shows hardness is a relative property.
items.answer: Rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron, showing that hardness is relative between different materials.

items.stem: Define transparent materials and give two examples.
items.answer: Transparent materials are those through which things can be seen clearly. Examples include glass, clean water, and air.

items.stem: Define opaque materials and give two examples.
items.answer: Opaque materials are those through which we cannot see at all. Examples include wood, cardboard, and metals.

items.stem: Define translucent materials and give two examples.
items.answer: Translucent materials are those through which objects can be seen, but not clearly. Butter paper and frosted glass are examples.

items.stem: What does it mean when we say a substance is ‘soluble’ in water? Give an example.
items.answer: A substance is soluble in water if it dissolves completely when mixed with water, like sugar or salt disappearing in water.

items.stem: What does it mean when we say a substance is ‘insoluble’ in water? Give an example.
items.answer: A substance is insoluble in water if it does not mix or disappear in water even after stirring, like sand or sawdust.

items.stem: Why is water important for the functioning of our body regarding solubility?
items.answer: Water is important because it can dissolve a large number of substances, which aids various bodily functions and transport of nutrients.

items.stem: Do all liquids mix with water? Explain briefly.
items.answer: No, not all liquids mix with water. Some, like vinegar, mix completely, while others, like oil, form a separate layer.

items.stem: How is an object with more mass different from an object with less mass in terms of heaviness?
items.answer: An object that is heavier has more mass, while an object that is lighter has less mass.

items.stem: What is volume, in the context of matter?
items.answer: Volume is the amount of space occupied by matter. For instance, the space water takes up in a bottle is its volume.

items.stem: What are the standard units mentioned for measuring mass?
items.answer: The standard units mentioned for measuring mass are gram (g) and kilogram (kg).

items.stem: What are the common units mentioned for measuring volume of liquids?
items.answer: Common units for measuring the volume of liquids are litre (L) and millilitre (mL).

items.stem: What is the SI unit for volume and its abbreviation?
items.answer: The SI unit for volume is cubic metre, and its abbreviation is m3

items.stem: How does the ‘materials’ in relation to ‘matter’?
items.answer: Materials are defined as types of matter that are used in the creation or making of objects.

items.stem: According to Ayurveda, how many principal properties (guna) are used to describe all physical matter?
items.answer: Ayurveda uses 20 principal properties (ten pairs of opposite properties) to describe all physical matter.

items.stem: Why is classification of objects and materials useful? Give an example of how grouping is done in a kitchen or a grocery shop.
items.answer: Classification is arranging objects into groups based on common properties, which helps in studying and observing patterns. In a kitchen, similar utensils are placed together. A grocer keeps all spices in one corner and grains in another, making them easy to locate and manage.

items.stem: Explain the concept of lustre with examples of lustrous and non-lustrous materials. Can a non- metallic material appear lustrous?
items.answer: Lustre refers to the shininess of a material’s surface. Metals like gold and copper are typically lustrous. non-lustrous materials like wood or paper lack this shine. Yes, a non-metallic material can appear lustrous if its surface is polished or coated with a shiny layer like plastic or wax.

items.stem: Describe the differences between transparent, translucent, and opaque materials. Provide one example for each category.
items.answer: Transparent materials allow clear visibility (e.g., glass).Translucent materials allow partial visibility, objects appear blurry (e.g., frosted glass).Opaque materials do not allow any light to pass through, so objects cannot be seen through them (e.g., a wooden door).

items.stem: What is meant by ‘solubility in water’? Describe an activity to show that some substances are soluble in water while others are not.
items.answer: Solubility is the property of a substance to dissolve in water. To test, take separate glass tumblers with water. Add sugar to one, salt to another, and sand to a third. Stir each. Sugar and salt will dissolve (soluble), while sand will not (insoluble), settling at the bottom.

items.stem: What is matter? What are the two fundamental properties that define matter? Mention the common units used to measure these properties.
items.answer: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. The two fundamental properties are mass and volume. Mass, the quantity of matter, is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg).Volume, the space occupied, is measured in litres (L) or millilitres (mL) for liquids.

items.stem: How did ancient Indian systems like Ayurveda classify physical matter? Briefly mention some of the properties they considered.
items.answer: Ancient Indian systems like Ayurveda classified matter based on 20 principal properties (guna), consisting of ten pairs of opposites. Some of these properties include heavy (guru) vs. light (laghu), cold (hima) vs. hot (ushna), smooth (shlakshana) vs. rough (khara), and soft (mridu) vs. hard (kathina).

items.stem: Why is it important to choose materials based on their properties for a specific use? Give an example of an object and explain why specific materials are chosen for its parts.
items.answer: Choosing materials based on properties ensures the object functions correctly and lasts. For example, a pen might use plastic for the body (lightweight, easy to mold), metal for the clip (strong, durable), and ink (flows, leaves a mark), each chosen for its specific function and properties.

items.stem: Describe how the Sindhu-Sarasvati (Harappan) Civilization showcased advanced techniques in pottery. What were these pots used for?
items.answer: The Harappan Civilization developed wheel- turned pottery, used pigmentation, applied protective/decorative multi-coloured ‘slips’, and painted black designs (geometric, animal motifs) on a red surface. Clay was carefully selected, cleaned, kneaded, wheeled, and baked in kilns (terracotta).Pots were used for cooking, and storing food grains, oil, and ghee.

items.stem: Explain why different types of balls used in sports are made of different materials. Relate this to their properties like bounce.
items.answer: Sports balls are made of specific materials due to the desired properties for that sport. For example, a tennis ball needs to be light and bouncy (high bounce), while a cricket ball is harder and has a different bounce characteristic. The material choice affects bounce, weight, and durability.

items.stem: What are the conventions for writing units of mass (kilogram) and volume (litre, millilitre, cubic metre) and their symbols according to the Do you know? sections?
items.answer: For ‘kg’, no space between ‘k’ and ‘g’, no full stop after symbol (unless at sentence end), space between number and ‘kg’.‘Litre’ is ‘L’, ‘millilitre’ is ‘mL’ (no space between m and L). ‘Cubic metre’ is ‘m 3 space between number and unit.

items.stem: A carpenter is making a table. He uses wood for the tabletop and legs, metal screws to join the parts, and varnish to coat the tabletop surface. He notices that the wood is hard, the metal screws are lustrous before use, and the varnish, when dried, gives a smooth and slightly shiny finish. (i) Why is wood, a hard material, a good choice for a tabletop and legs? (ii) The metal screws are lustrous. What does this property indicate about the screws, and why might they become dull over time? (iii) The varnish gives a smooth and shiny finish. Is the tabletop now considered a lustrous material because of the varnish? Explain. (Evaluating)
items.answer: (i) Wood is chosen for its hardness, meaning it is difficult to compress or scratch, providing strength and durability for the table’s structure and surface. (ii) The lustre indicates the screws are likely made of metal. They might become dull due to exposure to air and moisture, causing oxidation or tarnishing. (iii) The tabletop itself (wood) is non-lustrous, but the varnish coating makes its surface appear shiny. This doesn’t make the wood itself lustrous, but rather gives it a polished appearance.

items.stem: A chef is preparing a salad and a soup. For the salad, she uses fresh vegetables and a glass bowl. For the soup, she uses a metal pot for cooking on a stove. She observes that she can see the colorful vegetables clearly through the glass bowl. (i) What property of the glass bowl allows the chef to see the vegetables clearly? (ii) Why would a paper bowl be unsuitable for serving soup? (iii) The metal pot used for cooking soup is opaque. Why is this property acceptable for a cooking pot, unlike a serving bowl for salad?
items.answer: (i) The glass bowl is transparent, which means it allows light to pass through so things can be seen clearly. (ii) A paper bowl would be unsuitable for hot soup because paper is not strong enough when wet and would likely absorb the liquid, becoming soggy and leaking. (iii) Opaqueness is acceptable for a cooking pot because its primary function is to heat contents, not display them. For a salad bowl, transparency can be desirable for presentation.

items.stem: A student mixes sand, salt, and sugar in three separate beakers of water. After stirring, the salt and sugar disappear into the water, but the sand settles at the bottom. The student then pours the salt solution through a cloth filter. (i) Which substances are soluble in water, and which is insoluble? (ii) What property of salt and sugar allows them to disappear in water? (iii) Will the student be able to separate the dissolved salt from the water using the cloth filter? Why or why not?
items.answer: (i) Salt and sugar are soluble in water as they disappear. Sand is insoluble in water as it settles at the bottom. (ii) Their property of being soluble in water allows them to dissolve and disappear. (iii) No, the cloth filter will not separate the dissolved salt because the salt particles are too small and are evenly mixed (dissolved) in the water.

items.stem: Ghulan makes lemonade by mixing sugar, salt, and lemon juice in water. He observes that all these ingredients dissolve. Later, he notices water droplets forming on the outside of the cold glass of lemonade on a humid day. (i) Are sugar, salt, and lemon juice soluble or insoluble in water? (ii) What is the term for anything that has mass and occupies space, like the lemonade? (iii) The text discusses a similar phenomenon of water droplets on a cold glass. Where do these water droplets come from?
items.answer: (i) Sugar, salt and lemon juice are soluble in water as they dissolve to make the lemonade. (ii) Anything that has mass and occupies space, like the lemonade, is called matter. (iii) These water droplets come from the water vapour present in the surrounding air, which condenses on the cold outer surface of the glass.

items.stem: A factory needs to store different liquids: water, oil and acid. They need to choose appropriate container materials. They have containers made of glass, certain plastics, and uncoated steel. (i) For storing water, which of the listed materials would generally be suitable and why? (ii) If oil and water are stored together in one container, they form separate layers. Why is this? (iii) Why might uncoated steel be unsuitable for storing certain acids?
items.answer: (i) Glass and certain plastics are generally suitable for storing water as they can hold water without reacting with it or leaking. (ii) Oil and water form separate layers because oil does not mix with (is insoluble in) water. (iii) Uncoated steel might be unsuitable for storing certain acids because acids can react with metals like steel, causing corrosion and potentially contaminating the acid or damaging the container.
